content: Emerin is a protein in humans encoded by the EMD gene, also referred to as the STA gene. It is an integral protein of the inner nuclear membrane in vertebrates and contains a LEM domain, which it shares with LEMD3. Emerin is predominantly expressed in cardiac and skeletal muscle tissues. In cardiac muscle, it is localized to adherens junctions within intercalated discs, where it plays a role in mechanotransduction of cellular strain and beta-catenin signaling. Mutations in the emerin protein result in X-linked recessive Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and dilated cardiomyopathy. The protein is named after Alan Emery. Emerin is a 34 kDa protein (observed molecular weight) composed of 254 amino acids. It is serine-rich and contains an N-terminal hydrophobic region of 20 amino acids flanked by charged residues. This hydrophobic region is thought to anchor the protein to the membrane, while the charged terminal tails are cytosolic. In cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle, emerin is localized to the inner nuclear membrane, with the highest expression levels observed in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Specifically, in cardiac muscle, emerin is also found at adherens junctions within intercalated discs. Emerin is a serine-rich nuclear membrane protein and a member of the nuclear lamina-associated protein family. It mediates the anchorage of the nuclear membrane to the cytoskeleton. Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy is an X-linked inherited degenerative myopathy caused by mutations in the EMD (STA) gene. Emerin appears to be involved in mechanotransduction, as fibroblasts deficient in emerin fail to transduce normal mechanosensitive gene expression responses to strain stimuli. In cardiac muscle, emerin is complexed with beta-catenin at adherens junctions of intercalated discs. Cardiomyocytes from hearts lacking emerin exhibit beta-catenin redistribution, disrupted intercalated disc architecture, and altered myocyte shape. This interaction is regulated by glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta. Mutations in emerin cause X-linked recessive Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, which is characterized by early contractures in the Achilles tendons, elbows, and post-cervical muscles; muscle weakness that is proximal in the upper limbs and distal in the lower limbs; and cardiac conduction defects ranging from sinus bradycardia and PR prolongation to complete heart block. In affected patients, immunostaining for emerin is absent in various tissues, including muscle, skin fibroblasts, and leukocytes. However, diagnostic protocols rely on mutational analysis rather than protein staining. In nearly all cases, mutations result in a complete deletion or undetectable levels of emerin protein. Approximately 20% of cases involve X chromosomes with an inversion within the Xq28 region. Recent research suggests that the absence of functional emerin may reduce the infectivity of HIV-1. Consequently, it is speculated that patients with Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy may exhibit immunity to or an irregular infection pattern with HIV-1. Emerin has been shown to interact with several proteins, including ACTA1, ACTG2, BANF1, BCLAF1, CTNNB1, GMCL1, LMNA, PSME1, SYNE1, SYNE2, TMEM43, and YTHDC1.
